name: AWS CloudFront
description: Protects against destructive AWS CloudFront operations like deleting \ distributions, cache policies, and functions.

destructive_patterns.name: cloudfront-delete-distribution
destructive_patterns.description: aws cloudfront delete-distribution removes a CloudFront distribution.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a CloudFront distribution removes your CDN endpoint. All traffic \ to the distribution URL will fail. You must first disable the distribution \ and wait for propagation. Associated origins, behaviors, and cache settings \ are lost.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - aws cloudfront get-distribution: Review configuration first \ - Disable the distribution before deleting \ - Export the distribution config for backup

destructive_patterns.name: cloudfront-delete-cache-policy
destructive_patterns.description: aws cloudfront delete-cache-policy removes a cache policy.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a cache policy fails if any distribution behaviors reference it. \ If deletion succeeds, any caching optimizations you configured are lost. \ Custom TTLs, cache keys, and compression settings must be recreated.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - aws cloudfront get-cache-policy: Review policy settings first \ - Check which distributions use this policy \ - Create a replacement policy before deleting

destructive_patterns.name: cloudfront-delete-origin-request-policy
destructive_patterns.description: aws cloudfront delete-origin-request-policy removes an origin request policy.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting an origin request policy removes header, query string, and cookie \ forwarding configuration. Origins may receive different requests than \ expected, potentially breaking authentication or content negotiation.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - aws cloudfront get-origin-request-policy: Review settings first \ - Verify no distributions reference this policy \ - Create replacement before deletion

destructive_patterns.name: cloudfront-delete-function
destructive_patterns.description: aws cloudfront delete-function removes a CloudFront function.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a CloudFront Function removes edge compute logic. Any distributions \ using this function will lose URL rewriting, header manipulation, or other \ transformations. Function code is not recoverable after deletion.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - aws cloudfront get-function: Download function code first \ - Remove function associations from distributions first \ - Test replacements before deleting the original

destructive_patterns.name: cloudfront-delete-response-headers-policy
destructive_patterns.description: aws cloudfront delete-response-headers-policy removes a response headers policy.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a response headers policy removes security headers like CORS, \ Content-Security-Policy, and HSTS settings. Browsers may block cross-origin \ requests or report security warnings after deletion.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Review which distributions use this policy \ - Test your site without these headers in staging \ - Create a replacement policy before deleting

destructive_patterns.name: cloudfront-delete-key-group
destructive_patterns.description: aws cloudfront delete-key-group removes a key group used for signed URLs.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a key group breaks signed URL and signed cookie validation. \ Users with existing signed URLs will lose access to protected content. \ Any distributions using this key group for restricted content will deny \ all requests.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Rotate keys by adding new keys before removing old ones \ - Verify no distributions reference this key group \ - Update applications to use new signing keys first

destructive_patterns.name: cloudfront-create-invalidation
destructive_patterns.description: aws cloudfront create-invalidation creates a cache invalidation (has cost implications).
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Cache invalidations have cost implications after the first 1,000 paths per \ month. Wildcard invalidations (/*) count as one path but clear the entire \ cache, causing origin load spikes. Frequent invalidations defeat CDN benefits.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use versioned URLs (file.v2.js) instead of invalidation \ - Invalidate specific paths rather than wildcards \ - Set appropriate Cache-Control headers at the origin
